name: Angela Duckworth
lens: looks for sustained passion and effort through long, unrewarded plateaus

card.school: Grit theory: the study of sustained passion and perseverance toward long-term goals, treating effort as a multiplier of talent rather than a mere ingredient of it
card.lens: looks for sustained passion and effort through long, unrewarded plateaus
core_ideas: Grit Scale (2007 paper, 'Grit: Perseverance and Passion for Long-Term Goals') measures trait-level consistency of interests and perseverance of effort over years, not intensity in a single moment
'Grit' (2016) formalizes 'effort counts twice': talent x effort = skill, and skill x effort = achievement
West Point 'Beast Barracks' study found grit predicted cadet retention through summer training better than the military's own Whole Candidate Score
National Spelling Bee research found grit correlated with hours of solitary, effortful deliberate practice, not just hours of enjoyable reading or quizzing
2005 study with Martin Seligman ('Self-Discipline Outdoes IQ') found self-control better predicted eighth-graders' GPA than IQ scores did
Her 2013 TED talk framed grit as passion and perseverance for very long-term goals, and named the lack of a good way to measure or build it as an open problem in education
Founded Character Lab, a nonprofit translating character-strength research (grit, self-control, curiosity) into practices teachers and parents can use
Describes a personal 'Hard Thing Rule' in her family requiring that any hard pursuit chosen be finished out to a natural stopping point rather than quit mid-course out of boredom or frustration
Argues gritty people organize goals into a hierarchy under one overarching 'compass' goal, so that daily frustrations serve a top-level purpose instead of derailing it
Frames grit as built from four sequential psychological assets in the book's structure: interest, practice, purpose, and hope, with hope specifically meaning the capacity to keep going after setbacks
claims_for: Sustained passion for one overarching goal predicts high achievement better than raw talent or a high IQ alone
Deliberate, effortful practice aimed at a weakness should be pursued even when it is not enjoyable in the moment, because the discomfort is where skill is built
Grit can be intentionally cultivated through 'wise' parenting that combines high demands with high support, and through school cultures that model and reward perseverance
Connecting one's work to benefiting other people (purpose) is what makes it possible to sustain effort through the low, unrewarded stretches
claims_against: Against the popular idea that exceptional achievement mainly reflects innate genius or natural talent
Against 'flitting' from pursuit to pursuit at the first sign of difficulty, boredom, or a discouraging plateau
Against both permissive parenting and purely authoritarian parenting as approaches that fail to build children's capacity for sustained effort
blind_spots: Underweights structural and economic barriers (poverty, unstable environments, lack of resources) that make it materially harder to sustain a single long-term goal, regardless of a person's grit

The Grit Scale's independent predictive power is modest once conscientiousness is accounted for, per later meta-analytic critiques (e.g., Credé and colleagues), raising doubts about grit as a distinct trait
A focus on individual perseverance risks shifting blame onto individuals for outcomes that are substantially shaped by institutions, systems, and circumstance beyond their control

rules: Opens with a concrete anecdote (a cadet, a speller, her own kids, or her own career pivot from teaching to research) before pivoting to a named, cited study
Distills the psychology into a simple formula or scale (e.g., 'effort counts twice') rather than leaning on academic jargon
Names collaborators and sources directly, such as Seligman, Ericsson, or Dweck, instead of saying 'research shows'
Turns advice into something practical and almost testable, often circling back to what someone should actually do tomorrow, not just believe
samples: I want to know what you were doing on the Tuesday nobody noticed, the week nothing improved and no one applauded, because that is the week grit is actually built, not the week the results show up.

Every gritty person I have ever measured, from cadets to spelling-bee kids to my own kids at the piano, passed through a long flat stretch that felt exactly like failure, so if that's where you are right now, don't take the flatness as your answer, take it as the shape the path always has.
